query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled, low‐temperature pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, uniform, and adherent HfO2 surface scale will significantly improve the high‐temperature oxygen resistance of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr without adversely affecting its intrinsic ductility and yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a single pre-oxidation treatment by heating the alloy at 600–700 °C under a controlled, low oxygen partial pressure for approximately 1 hour to form a thin protective HfO2 surface layer.
generation.conditions: Pre-oxidation at 600–700 °C in an atmosphere with reduced oxygen content (controlled oxygen partial pressure) for ~1 hour; subsequent high-temperature performance evaluation at up to 1000 °C in an oxidizing environment (e.g., air) under tensile loading with strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ over extended exposure times representative of service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent HfO2 surface scale that acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed HfO2 scale is expected to passivate the alloy’s surface by limiting oxygen ingress during high-temperature exposure. This barrier prevents deep oxidation of the subsurface regions while preserving the as-cast bulk microstructure, thereby maintaining the alloy’s high-temperature yield strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the pre-oxidized alloy will exhibit a significantly reduced oxidation depth and minimized embrittlement during prolonged exposure at high temperatures (up to 1000 °C) under tensile stress, while retaining comparable ductility and yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy which shows poor oxygen resistance, leading to deep oxygen ingress and embrittlement under high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.boundary: The intervention is limited to surface treatment via pre-oxidation (without any bulk thermomechanical processing). It is effective as long as the HfO2 scale remains stable and adherent under the specified high-temperature tensile loading conditions (strain rates of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ and exposures up to 1000 °C).
generation.uncertainty: Optimal pre-oxidation parameters (exact temperature within the 600–700 °C range, oxygen partial pressure, and duration) and the long-term adhesion and stability of the HfO2 layer under cyclic or sustained tensile loading remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one set subjected to the controlled pre-oxidation treatment (600–700 °C, controlled low oxygen partial pressure, 1 hour) and a control set left untreated. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature conditions (up to 1000 °C in air) while applying tensile loads at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹ over extended durations. Perform surface and cross-sectional microstructural analyses before and after testing.
measurements: Thickness, uniformity, and continuity of the HfO2 scale (via SEM/EDS or TEM)
Oxygen penetration depth in the subsurface (using cross-sectional analysis)
High-temperature tensile properties (yield strength and ductility)
Fractographic analysis to detect oxidation-induced embrittlement
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidation treatment does not result in a continuous, thin HfO2 scale that effectively limits oxygen penetration (i.e., no significant difference in oxide depth between treated and untreated samples) or if the treated samples display reduced yield strength or ductility relative to the untreated ones under high-temperature tensile testing, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In this paper, we designed and prepared All7Cr10Fe36−xNi36Mo1Hfx dual-phase high-entropy alloys (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 in at%) with FCC and B2 phases. Firstly, the same thermal and mechanical treatment was conducted on the All7Cr10Fe36−xNi36Mo1Hfx cast alloy to eliminate segregation and solidification defects in the cast alloy. Then, a systematic study was conducted on the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the All7Cr10Fe36−xNi36Mo1Hfx alloy. The addition of Hf can simultaneously improve the high-temperature strength and ductility of the matrix alloy in the temperature range from 600 °C to 900 °C, especially at 700 °C. The strengthening and toughening mechanisms at 700 °C in the All7Cr10Fe35.5Ni36Mo1Hf0.5 alloys were analyzed by comparing the differences in fracture behavior and microstructure between the Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1 and Al17Cr10Fe35.5Ni36Mo1Hf0.5 alloys.

The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo. decision.trend: Early studies in the HfNbTaTiZr system and its derivatives focused predominantly on optimizing the core mechanical properties—balancing high tensile strength at elevated temperatures with acceptable ductility—by tuning elemental combinations and controlling microstructure (e.g., avoiding deleterious phase segregation from Ta and Zr co‐presence). While these works successfully characterized and improved mechanical performance in the as‐cast state through compositional adjustments and thermomechanical treatments, they did not address environmental degradation issues. In parallel, other high-entropy and medium-entropy alloy investigations using microalloying (such as Hf additions in other alloy systems) have shown that modifying the microstructure externally or near the surface may enhance high-temperature performance by arresting deleterious mechanisms, yet the oxidation problem remained unsolved.
decision.unsolved: No prior study on the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy has provided a single, practical intervention to enhance its oxygen resistance in high-temperature oxidative atmospheres without impacting its intrinsic mechanical properties. The challenge is to prevent deep oxygen ingress during prolonged exposure at up to 1000 °C while preserving the alloy's as-cast microstructure and mechanical behavior under tensile loading.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled, low-temperature pre-oxidation treatment designed to form a thin, uniform, and adherent Hf-rich oxide (HfO2) scale on the alloy surface
decision.why: This approach draws on the trend that many high-entropy alloy studies focusing on performance improvements have left environmental resistance unaddressed. By engineering a protective surface layer through a pre-oxidation process—applied under controlled oxygen partial pressures and at moderate temperatures to allow formation of a stable, passivating HfO2 barrier—the intervention isolates oxidation to the surface without altering the as-cast bulk microstructure, thereby preserving the alloy's ductility and high-temperature yield strength. Such a pre-formed oxide layer would limit further oxygen ingress during extended exposure at service temperatures (up to 1000 °C) under tensile load, and its effectiveness could be falsified by comparing oxidation kinetics and mechanical performance between treated and untreated specimens over prolonged high-temperature oxidative testing.
